issues.title: Why Cement Costs So Much
issues.subtitle: Nigeria produces way more cement than it uses. Cement still sells for less in several other African markets. The FCCPC just published preliminary findings from a three-month study, and found exactly what you'd expect. This issue is about what that means for anyone trying to build, rent, or just stay housed.
issues.body:
Between January and July this year, a 50kg bag of cement went from about ₦9,300 to as much as ₦15,000 in some places. The usual suspects got blamed: fuel subsidy removal, the dollar rate, diesel for haulage, inflation. All real. But this week, the Federal Competition and Consumer Protection Commission published preliminary findings from a three-month study and found something else going on too.

Nigeria isn't short of cement. We sit on massive limestone deposits across Kogi, Ogun, Edo, and Sokoto. Local factories have an estimated 60 to 65 million tonnes of installed capacity a year and domestic demand is estimated at 25 to 30 million. That's a serious surplus. And yet cement often sells for less in other African markets than it does to Nigerians buying from a factory down the road.

The numbers make it plain: ₦13,000–15,000 a bag here in July 2026. ₦9,300 in January. And Kenya, which has its own cement industry, was paying the equivalent of about ₦7,344 a bag.

So what's happening? Three companies: Dangote, BUA, and Lafarge (now HBM Nigeria) account for more than 90 percent of installed production capacity. When three players hold that much of anything, prices can jump fast when input costs rise and barely move when things settle. While ordinary Nigerians were freezing their building projects, the top producers' annual reports were showing record revenue and healthy margins.

And this isn't the first time someone tried to fix it. In February 2024, those same three companies agreed with the government that prices should sit around ₦7,000 to ₦8,000 a bag. That agreement fell apart within months. Prices kept climbing anyway.

Here's why it hits harder than just a building material going up in price. For someone earning between ₦70,000 and ₦120,000 a month, even a modest two-bedroom bungalow can need hundreds of bags of cement. At ₦13,000 a bag, 200 bags alone would cost ₦2.6 million before you've bought sand, granite, iron rods, or paid a single mason.

The bigger problem is that Nigeria has a tiny mortgage market. Outstanding mortgages amount to less than 1 percent of the economy here, far below countries with deeper housing-finance systems. So many of us who want to own something don't borrow to build, we save cash and buy blocks little by little over years. When cement prices move like this, the money saved for 100 bags in January buys only about 60 bags by July. The plan doesn't just slow down. It breaks.

Add a housing shortage now estimated at close to 15 million homes, and owning property, the one thing that used to offer some financial security in old age is turning into something you can only dream about instead of actually plan for.

Cement prices also feed directly into rent. New apartments get priced against today's cost of building, which is part of how basic flats in Lagos or Abuja end up demanding ₦1.5 million to ₦3 million upfront. And older flats aren't exempt either, 'cement and building costs' still gets pulled out as the reason for a rent hike at renewal, whether the excuse holds up or not.

That's the loop: we can't afford to build, so we rent, and the same cement prices keeping us from owning become the excuse landlords use to raise what we pay for someone else's place.

The FCCPC inquiry is the real test now. Can regulatory pressure actually force fair prices, or will three companies keep deciding whether our generation ever gets to own the roof over our heads?

issues.title: Nigeria Uses AI but doesn’t own any of it
issues.followTitle: Nigeria Uses AI but doesn’t own any of it
issues.subtitle: Nearly nine in ten Nigerian adults surveyed online said they had used AI chatbots, one of the highest adoption rates Google and Ipsos measured. Much of it runs on servers, models and currencies Nigeria does not control. This issue is about the gap between adoption and ownership.
issues.body:
Nigeria just topped a major survey on AI chatbot use. Nearly nine in ten Nigerian adults surveyed online said they had used one, more than any other country Google and Ipsos measured. That's a wild stat. It's also only half the story.

Because much of that usage runs on infrastructure Nigeria doesn't own. Many of the servers are abroad. Most of the biggest models were built abroad. The bills often come in dollars. We're among the world's heaviest users of a technology we still have a limited stake in.

There's a real cost to that. Kasi Cloud estimates that Nigerian enterprises spend $850 million every year on foreign cloud infrastructure. Much of that money leaves and doesn't come back.

The pricing situation is its own headache. Many Nigerian debit cards still don't work reliably for international subscriptions, so people go through virtual dollar cards from apps like Grey or Chipper Cash. A $20 AI tool can cost more than a straight conversion at the official rate once the provider's exchange rate and fees are added. Meanwhile, some services offer lower-priced plans through Nigerian app stores. Same month. Very different bill depending on the tool and how you pay.

Something is moving on the infrastructure side, though. The government is trying to draw hundreds of millions of dollars into cloud and data-centre infrastructure at home. Kasi Cloud is one of the projects coming online. If it works, more of that spending can stay in Nigeria instead.

But data centers are just buildings. The harder question is whether Nigeria can build the actual AI, the models, not just the infrastructure underneath them.

Honestly? The talent is already there. Nigeria has a growing crop of AI startups. Terra Industries in Abuja builds AI-enabled drones and says its systems are used across eight African countries and Canada. Awarri built N-ATLAS, a set of open-source models that work across Yoruba, Hausa, Igbo and Nigerian-accented English, something most foreign labs never bothered with.

The gap isn't the people. It's everything around them. Only about 5 percent of African AI talent has access to the computing power needed for research and innovation. Structured AI programmes also remain limited across many African universities. And the engineers Nigeria trains keep getting picked up by foreign companies paying in dollars, which makes it hard for local startups to hold onto them.

AI is already being put to work here, by the way. Traffic projects are testing it against congestion. Farming tools are helping some farms make better decisions about crops and water. Health teams are exploring it to spot risks earlier. That's not just future talk, it's starting to happen now.

The problem is that many of these systems still rely on tools Nigeria doesn't control. If a foreign provider changes its pricing or cuts access, a traffic system, farming app or diagnostic tool could be disrupted. And most of these tools were built for English speakers first, so the gains for people working in Hausa, Yoruba or Igbo can be smaller than the headline numbers suggest.

Nigeria is very good at using AI. The next question is how much of it we can build and own ourselves.

issues.title: The Boom Nobody Can Feel
issues.subtitle: Lagos had just become the best-performing stock market among 92 exchanges tracked by Bloomberg. The naira was steadier, inflation was easing, foreign investors were trickling back. None of that meant your money went further, and this issue is about the gap between the two.
issues.body:
At the time this went out, the numbers looked good. Inflation was easing. The naira was steadier. Foreign investors were trickling back. And Nigeria's stock market had just become the best-performing exchange among the 92 Bloomberg tracked, up about 67 percent in dollar terms since January.

But go to any market in Lagos and ask how people are feeling. The answer won't match those headlines.

So what's actually going on?

The stock market rally is real, but it's not random. Three things happened at once. The Central Bank told banks to raise fresh capital, so they went back to the stock market to do it, and investors followed. The naira float and subsidy removal, brutal as they were in 2023, are finally producing some of the stability economists said they would. And much of the money driving this rally is Nigerian, not foreign: pension funds, domestic institutions chasing yield. Foreign investors are coming back, but slowly.

Which means this is a very specific kind of boom. It's moving between banks, pension funds and big companies. Ecobank up 127 percent. Zenith up nearly 78 percent. Jaiz Bank up over 82 percent. If you're not inside that loop, you're watching it from outside.

And outside that loop, things are rough. Nearly 35 million Nigerians are facing acute hunger this lean season, the worst in a decade. About 3 million children under five are at risk of severe malnutrition this year alone.

Street-level crime feels bolder too. In Lagos, agbero extortion was back in the news after a viral clip of area boys blocking a wedding convoy and damaging the car when the driver refused to pay. One clip isn't a national crime index, but daylight intimidation in traffic is familiar enough to land.

Here's the thing about inflation 'easing': it just means prices are rising slower. Not that anything got cheaper. Many salaries haven't kept pace. So even as the macro numbers improve, most people's money still buys less than it did last year.

Tinubu bet his presidency on Nigerians accepting short-term pain for long-term gain. Three years on, some of the reform math is working on paper. But most people still can't feel it at their kitchen table. Nigeria votes again on January 16, 2027, and that gap, between the stock ticker and the grocery bill, is the whole election.

issues.title: The US Visa Squeeze
issues.subtitle: Three separate US visa policy moves landed in the same few weeks, and none of them made one big scary headline alone. One was later blocked in court. Read together, they still tell you where this is going.
issues.body:
There was no big announcement. No single ban. Just three separate policy updates, dropped weeks apart, each one easy to miss on its own. Together, they pointed in the same direction.

First: Abuja lost routine visa processing. From August 1, the US realigned those services from its Abuja embassy, one of 25 posts across Africa affected by the change. The embassy itself stayed open, but Lagos became Nigeria's routine visa hub. One office. More than 200 million people.

To be clear, this touches both immigrant and nonimmigrant visas, including tourist and business visas. The people affected include holiday and business travellers as well as those trying to move permanently: family visas, employment-based applications, DV lottery winners, fiancé visas. Think of it like closing one of two toll gates on the Lagos-Ibadan expressway. Same destination, one lane. Queues get longer. Appointments get slower.

Second: student status was set to get a hard deadline. F-1 students used to be able to stay as long as they were making academic progress, no fixed end date. A rule scheduled for September 15 would have given new students a maximum of four years, with 30 days to arrive before classes start and 30 days to leave after the period ends.

Four years is fine for most undergrad programmes. It's tight for medicine, engineering, or a PhD. Students in longer courses would have had to apply for extensions mid-study, and approval wasn't guaranteed. The grace period after graduation would also have dropped from 60 days to 30. More than 20,000 Nigerian students were enrolled in the US in the 2024/25 academic year.

That rule did not take effect on September 15. A federal judge blocked it while a legal challenge continues, so the old duration-of-status system and 60-day grace period remain in place for now.

Third: the visa itself is now single-use. This one actually came first, quietly, in July 2025. Most new US visas issued to Nigerians are now valid for just three months and allow one entry. Once you leave the US, that visa is done. Coming back, even to the same university, means applying for a new one from scratch. Visas issued before July 2025 are fine. New ones aren't.

None of these moves alone is a ban. Even with the student rule on hold, the others make the process slower, more expensive, and a lot less forgiving. If you're planning to study or move to the US, start earlier than you think you need to. That's not just advice anymore, it's the new reality.

issues.title: The NYSC Reform Everyone Missed
issues.subtitle: NYSC almost swapped khaki for Adire this week. Far fewer people noticed the actual reform hiding right behind it: the biggest shake-up to the scheme in 53 years.
issues.body:
NYSC's khaki uniform might soon become Adire, the tie-dye fabric our aunty wears to owambes. The Minister of Youth Development, Ayodele Olawande, said it live on Channels TV's The Morning Brief, and Nigerian Twitter did what Nigerian Twitter does.

"It's Adire. Adire is being produced in Nigeria. We have them in Ogun, we have them in Kwara, we have textile industry. Let's put our money back into the country," he said.

Some people loved it. Local textile makers in Ogun and Kwara finally getting a national moment. Others weren't having it: why should a national uniform lean on a fabric tied to one region? By evening, Olawande walked it back. Adire and Ankara were just examples floated during consultations, not a done deal. Khaki lives to see another day, for now.

But the uniform was never really the story. It's one small piece of the biggest NYSC shake-up in 53 years, quietly approved by the Federal Executive Council the same week. Camp orientation doubles from three weeks to six. The Passing Out Parade becomes a graduation ceremony. A civilian takes over day-to-day leadership, with the military still handling security.

The change that actually matters though: corps members might finally get posted to places that match what they studied. Right now NYSC can mean a whole year doing nothing related to your degree. A Computer Science grad teaching Basic Science. An Agriculture grad filing paperwork. A Medical Lab Science grad who never sees the inside of a hospital.

If postings matched qualifications, everyone involved could benefit: graduates get real experience, organisations get skills they're already paying for. The catch, and there's always one, is that not every local government has a slot for every course. Matching roughly 400,000 graduates a year to the right roles is less a policy win and more a massive logistics problem. But at least someone's finally trying.
